'''Susan Jane Cunningham''' (March 23, 1842 – January 24, 1921) was an American mathematician instrumental in the founding and development of [[Swarthmore College]].<ref name="agnesscott1">{{cite web|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/cunning.htm |title=Susan Jane Cunningham |work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians |publisher=Agnes Scott College |access-date=2012-10-24}}</ref> She was born in [[Maryland]], and studied mathematics and astronomy with [[Maria Mitchell]] at [[Vassar College]] as a [[Matriculation#Special student|special student]] during 1866–67.<ref name="agnesscott1"/> She also studied those subjects during several summers at [[Harvard University]], [[Princeton University]], [[Newnham College, Cambridge]], the [[Royal Observatory, Greenwich]], and [[Williams College]].<ref name="agnesscott1"/>

==Early life and education==
Mary Jane Cunningham was born in [[Harford County, Maryland]], March 23, 1842. On her mother's side she was of Quaker descent. Her mother died in 1845, and Susan was left to the care of her grandparents.{{sfn|Willard|Livermore|1893|p=221}}

She attended a Friends' school until she was fifteen years old, when it was decided that she should prepare for the work of teaching. She was sent to a Friends' boarding-school in [[Montgomery County, Maryland]] for a year, when family cares required her to return home, and she continued her studies in the school near by.{{sfn|Willard|Livermore|1893|p=221}}

At nineteen, she became a teacher, and she has taught thereafter, with the exception of two years, one of which she spent in the Friends' school in [[Newtown Friends School|Leghorne]], or Attleboro, and the other in Vassar College. She spent her summer vacations in study. She studied in [[Harvard College Observatory]] in the summers of 1874 and 1876, in Princeton observatory in 1881, in Williamstown in 1883 and 1884, under Prof. [[Truman Henry Safford]], and in Cambridge, England, in 1877, in 1878, in 1879 and in 1882, under a private tutor. In 1887, she studied in the [[Cambridge Observatory]], England, and in 1891, she spent the summer in the Greenwich, England, observatory.{{sfn|Willard|Livermore|1893|p=221}}

==Career==
In 1869, she became one of the founders of the mathematics and astronomy departments at Swarthmore, and she headed both those divisions until her retirement in 1906.<ref name="google1">{{cite book|last=Schlup|first=Leonard C.|title=Historical Dictionary of the Gilded Age|year=2003|publisher=M.E. Sharpe|location=Armonk, N.Y.|isbn=978-0-7656-0331-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lhRqUo9HzVwC&q=%22susan+jane+cunningham%22&pg=PA546|author2=Ryan, James G. |page=546}}</ref> She was Swarthmore's first professor of astronomy, and was professor of mathematics at the college beginning in 1871.<ref name="agnesscott1"/><ref name="swarthmore1">{{cite web|last=Weber |first=Elizabeth |url=http://www.sccs.swarthmore.edu/users/98/elizw/Swat.history/Cunningham.html |title=The Cunningham Building: Swarthmore's Other Observatory |work=The Phoenix |publisher=Swarthmore College |date=November 15, 1996 |access-date=2012-10-24}}</ref> By 1888, she was Mathematics Department Chair, and that year she was given permission to plan and equip the first observatory in Swarthmore, which housed the astronomy department, and in which she lived in until her retirement; it was known as Cunningham Observatory.<ref name="agnesscott1"/><ref name="swarthmore1"/> The building still exists on the campus although it is no longer used as an observatory, and is now simply known as the Cunningham Building.<ref name="agnesscott1"/><ref name="swarthmore1"/> In 1888, Cunningham was given the first honorary doctorate of science ever given by Swarthmore.<ref name="google1"/> In 1891, she became one of the first six women to join the New York Mathematical Society, which later became the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="google2">{{cite book|last=Duren|first=Peter L.|title=A Century of Mathematics in America|year=1990|publisher=American Mathemat. Soc.|location=Providence, RI|isbn=978-0-8218-0130-7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Eq5072shy9AC&q=%22susan+jane+cunningham%22+math&pg=PA382|edition=2. [Dr.]|author2=Askey, Richard |author3=Merzbach, Uta C.|author3-link= Uta Merzbach |page=382}}</ref> The very first was [[Charlotte Angas Scott]], and the other four were [[Mary E. Byrd]] of [[Smith College]], [[Mary Watson Whitney]] of [[Vassar College|Vassar]], [[Ellen Hayes]] of [[Wellesley College|Wellesley]], and Amy Rayson, who taught mathematics and physics at a private school in New York City.<ref name="google2"/> Cunningham was also a member of the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]] as early as 1891.<ref>{{cite journal|title=List of Members of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific|jstor=40666804|journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|volume=3|issue=13|date=January 1, 1891|pages=1–8}}</ref> She was also a founder member of the British Astronomical Association in 1890, resigned 1908 September. She was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1901.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic|title=Historic Fellows|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|access-date=2021-04-21}}</ref>

==Death==
Cunningham died on January 24, 1921, from heart failure. Her funeral service was held on-campus in the Swarthmore College Meeting House, and was attended by many notable figures such as then-Pennsylvania governor [[William Cameron Sproul|William C. Sproul]] and Pennsylvania State Commissioner of Health Edward Martin.<ref>{{cite news|title=Funeral of Dr. Cunningham|url=http://triptych.brynmawr.edu/cdm/compoundobject/collection/SC_Phoenix2/id/6733/rec/78|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140327164705/http://triptych.brynmawr.edu/cdm/compoundobject/collection/SC_Phoenix2/id/6733/rec/78|url-status=dead|archive-date=2014-03-27|access-date=2014-03-27|newspaper=The Phoenix|date=February 8, 1921}}</ref>
